dots.s: He trained image classifiers and object detectors from scratch in PyTorch and exported them to run on a phone.
The training is the ordinary part.
The care went into evaluation: a validation set frozen so leakage is impossible, and a gate that rejects a model with a better average score if any single class got meaningfully worse.
Three OCR engines in one pipeline, each doing what it is genuinely good at rather than being treated as interchangeable.
One is used only to locate where text sits on the page, because its transcription cannot be trusted.
A field is confirmed only when two passes agree, so it reports what it could not read instead of guessing.
Supporting work rather than a project in its own right, but it is what the vision models were trained on.
He built an in-house annotation tool for the labelling, and used Roboflow alongside it where that was the faster path.
Thousands of label files went through it, and the models on this site were trained on what came out.
The models run on the device because the people using them are standing in a paddock with no signal.
Image preprocessing is baked into the exported model, so it cannot drift from the training code
Updates arrive over the air and are checksum-verified before the swap
Any failure falls back to the bundled model, so a bad release cannot break it
Speech in and out, in production rather than in a demo, and across languages.
OpenAI Whisper for speech to text, running in two separate systems
ElevenLabs for streaming voice, with the latency optimisation on and settings tuned per persona
OpenAI text to speech, and AWS Polly generative voices on another product
Multilingual, which matters on a factory floor where not everyone reads English
All of it sits behind one voice abstraction, so switching provider is a config change.
Each vendor uses a different valid range for the same setting, and those are normalised into one column, so adding a provider does not mean a schema migration.
His biggest and most current work.
A conversational avatar on a kiosk and on the web, answering from a company's own documents.
Claude for the brain, over hybrid retrieval: vector search alongside keyword ranking
Two modes, and the difference is who does the work.
Full mode has the vendor do the speech and the model.
Lite renders video only at half the rate
The kiosk runs on lite, so that stack is ours: the visitor's phone as the microphone, streaming speech to text, our own voice
Multilingual, with face recognition at the kiosk
Around 660 commits, live, trialled on site with several hundred staff.
Two shapes of the same idea.
A photoreal avatar you can hold a spoken conversation with, backed by a language model and hybrid retrieval
An illustrated one delivering the same conversation through a drawn character.
It starts from illustrated stills of a person, then the parts that move are rigged separately, the eyes and the mouth, and driven by the conversation in the browser
Built in TypeScript and React.
No 3D head and no render farm, so a client can have a character in their own house style without the pipeline that usually implies.
Genuinely hybrid rather than hybrid in name.
A dense vector search runs alongside ordinary keyword ranking, and the two result lists are fused
Source links travel with each passage into the model's context, so an answer cites something real
It distinguishes found nothing from could not run, so a failure is never disguised as an empty result
He built a multi-tenant agent runtime where the model calls real tools rather than only generating text: retrieving documents, producing PDFs, sending email.
The decision worth knowing is where authorisation lives.
It is enforced in the API, never in the prompt, because a model will eventually be talked into attempting something it was never granted.
He has used LangChain and LangGraph, though the systems on this site are built directly on the model SDKs rather than through a framework.

The orchestration is there either way: a model router as a tested pure function with eight named decision paths, thread-level state so a conversation that escalated stays escalated, and a fallback ladder that separates retrieval found nothing from retrieval could not run
Every routing decision comes back on the response itself, so the path taken is observable from the client without a logging round trip
Going direct keeps every cost and latency lever reachable, and it means he knows what a framework is doing underneath rather than only how to call it
Retrieval over a corpus he wrote, not an agent.
Most questions are answered from a hand-reviewed set with no model call at all, so this costs nothing to run and cannot be used as a free model proxy.

A genuinely new question goes to a model running inside the same Cloudflare account, and the shape of the question decides which one: short and plainly worded gets a small fast model, long or multi-part gets a much larger one.
When something falls outside the corpus I say so, which is the same thing his systems do.
Cloud is half of what he does, not a footnote to the model.
AWS is his area of expertise, and he has delivered client work on Azure and Google Cloud as well.
Serverless AWS: Lambda behind API Gateway and CloudFront, with Postgres and S3 underneath
All of it in infrastructure as code across two regions, not clicked together in a console
Four Lambda packaging strategies running side by side, each chosen for a stated reason
His degree majored in cloud computing before any of it was a job, which is why he tends to reach for the networking and distributed systems half first.
AWS is the estate he knows best, and he has owned it rather than used it.
Lambda, S3 and CloudFront are the three he is deepest in, alongside ECS, EC2, API Gateway, Aurora Serverless v2, DynamoDB and Bedrock, defined as code with CDK
Container orchestration across ECS and EKS, with Fargate where a managed control plane is the right trade
Solved the deploy size limit three separate times, three different ways
Removed a database proxy costing about $144 a month, on measured evidence
Australian regions for client compliance.
Also delivered on Azure and Google Cloud.
Delivery and automation are things he owns, not an afterthought.
CI on GitLab CI and GitHub Actions across the repos
Docker and Docker Compose, so local and production run the same image
Lambda shipped two ways, a zip build and a container image from ECR, so a service past the size limit still deploys
Front ends go out as an S3 sync with a CloudFront invalidation, releases tagged for a named rollback target
Retraining, promotion, export and versioning run as one automated path, and a cloud GPU training job stops itself
Headless mobile build pipelines mean an app rebuilds from a script, not one machine.
AWS is his area of expertise, but he has worked across all three major clouds for clients.
Client work on Azure and Google Cloud, not just exposure to them
Migrations off Azure and Google Cloud onto AWS, taken end to end
Doing that meant working with the equivalent service on both sides, because you cannot move something you do not understand
The useful part is knowing which concepts hold everywhere and which are genuinely provider-specific.
AWS is where he goes deepest, and the other two are real experience rather than a line on a CV.
Python and FastAPI across his platforms, over async SQLAlchemy and PostgreSQL, with TypeScript, Next.js and React for the interfaces.
PostgreSQL with pgvector for the retrieval systems
MongoDB Atlas behind the analytics platform, sitting behind a private link
Roughly 150 hand-written migrations shipped alongside the features that needed them
He has rebuilt user sessions from events that arrived duplicated and out of order, which is the kind of problem that only exists once real traffic is hitting the thing.
Cost is a design constraint, not something to apologise for afterwards.
A router picks the cheapest model that can answer, and escalates only when the question earns it
Idle sessions close themselves, so an abandoned tab stops billing
Spend caps pause the expensive call while keeping search working
Transcription moved in-process, removing a per-minute bill entirely
The biggest by a distance is a conversational avatar, on a kiosk and on the web, answering from a company's own documents.
Around 660 commits, live in front of real users.
Alongside it:
A retrieval assistant that answers a question asked as text, speech or a photograph, with real source links
Computer vision models trained from scratch and run on the phone itself, because the users have no signal
An analytics platform turning millions of messy events into something you can query
Some of that work was his alone, plenty of it shared with other engineers and designers.
More than seventy since January 2024, counting only the repositories he has actually committed work into.
Fourteen of those are AI or machine learning systems.
The rest is the platform work underneath them: the APIs, the pipelines, the databases and the cloud they run on.
Retrieval and LLM application engineering are the deepest, with cloud architecture close behind.

The less common part is the range: on the systems he has owned outright, the same person trains the model, writes the API, designs the schema and runs the infrastructure, so decisions at each layer are made with the others in view.
He has also worked as one of several engineers on shared platforms, so it is not only a solo skill set.
He is an AI software engineer.
A lot of his work has been solo, where a day runs the whole depth of one system rather than one layer of several: the model, the API, the schema and the deploy.
Plenty of it has been collaborative too, working alongside other engineers and designers on a shared platform.
Two habits show up either way:
He measures before changing something, so a saving or a model swap comes with the numbers behind it
He writes down what a system cannot do, not only what it can
Anything beyond that is his to answer rather than mine.
Both, and he is clear about which is which.
Several systems he owned outright, from the model through to the deployed infrastructure
Plenty of other work shared with engineers, designers and Unity developers on the same platform
He has also picked up someone else's codebase, audited it, and shipped fixes into it
The solo work is where the depth comes from.
The shared work is why the solo work has tests, migrations and documentation rather than only being in his head.
